content: Healthcare workers should aim to simplify processes to prevent patients from avoiding hepatitis C virus (HCV) care. Additionally, HCV testing and treatment should be integrated into routine health services available to the general public, such as family medicine, as well as into specialized services targeting specific groups, such as maternity care, harm-reduction programs, tuberculosis clinics, or HIV clinics. However, while these recommendations are intended to address barriers to HCV testing and treatment, informants have cautioned that improper planning and a lack of sensitivity to community needs and preferences could inadvertently create new barriers. For example, decentralizing services to clinics with inadequate infrastructure and poor organization may lead to low acceptance by patients. Similarly, shifting tasks to healthcare workers who are already avoided by affected populations will not increase HCV testing uptake. Furthermore, integrating HCV testing into services that are avoided by at-risk groups, such as HIV clinics avoided by some LGBTQ+ individuals, may fail to improve testing rates. In all these scenarios, point-of-care (PoC) or near-point-of-care testing will be essential. Informants emphasized the need for immediate confirmatory testing, which requires PoC viral load (VL) testing. Acknowledgments are extended to the NGOs and community-based organizations that played a critical role in identifying and recruiting participants for this assessment, as well as to the field staff who conducted and documented interviews and participatory research sessions. Special thanks are given to the participants for sharing their personal experiences and insights. Gratitude is also extended to the lead consultants from various countries, including Brazil, Costa Rica, India, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, the Philippines, Rwanda, South Africa, Thailand, and Ukraine, for their contributions to exploring values and preferences regarding HCV self-testing. This assessment was part of the HEAD-Start project, supported by UNITAID and the Government of the Netherlands. The protocol and guiding materials for the rapid qualitative assessment were developed by Guillermo Z. Martínez Pérez (FIND), with technical support provided to in-country consultants. The report was developed in collaboration with Sonjelle Shilton, who conceptualized the initial assessment. References include studies and systematic reviews on the decentralization, integration, and task-shifting of HCV testing and treatment, as well as the usability and acceptability of HCV self-testing in various populations and regions.
